#29835. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers.
  • It has been revealed that back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades.
  • The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

It has been revealed that back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:.

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

It has been revealed that that’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

According to recent reports, but it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:.

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Industry observers note that tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Industry observers note that through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:.

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

Industry observers note that as we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We noted to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

According to recent reports, we don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

Sources indicate that the real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a fresh car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch newly introduced models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

Latest Update: TikTok’s Viral Winter Arc Challenge Is the Best Way to Get a Jump-Start on Your New Year’s Goals

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year.
  • That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play.
  • This time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, states Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in New York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year. While, yes, you should cut yourself some slack here and there during the busy holiday season, it’s also more crucial now than ever to finish the year strong.

That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play. This annual challenge, which originally went viral on TikTok back in 2024, starts October 1 and ends January 1 (but if you missed the start, it’s not too late!). The only premise: Stay locked in on your goals for the rest of the calendar year, whether that’s training for a half-marathon, hitting your Goodreads book quota, or mastering a new hobby.

This time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, states Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in New York City. Now’s the time for you to “be intentional about your energy and what serves you.”.

In a recent development, if you haven’t started the challenge yet, it’s not too late. Whether you try it for 83 or 30 days, the Winter Arc Challenge will set you up for greater success with your Newly introduced Year’s goals because it’ll strengthen your self-efficacy, or “your sense of belief in your own ability to do what you say that you are going to do,” notes Carmichael. Self-efficacy is strengthened through your own behavioral track record, so if you start meeting goals now, you’ll already have momentum heading into January, she explains.

Sources indicate that ready to tackle your own Winter Arc Challenge? Here are some helpful tips to help you make the most of the next few months:.

Maybe as part of your Winter Arc Challenge, you aim to cut your monthly spending in half. But a few weeks after setting this goal, you really go overboard at brunches and parties. Don't sweat it. This is “a completely normal part of the change process,” Carmichael claims. Instead of giving up when you encounter a relapse here or there, strategy for bumps to happen, then get back on track.

Industry observers note that so, if you spend too much money one week, instead of falling into a pattern of negative self-talk, replace your thoughts. Carmichael says to proposal a script of what you can say to yourself when you relapse, like: “I can still get back on track and feel good about my goals. This is my moment to restart.”.

According to recent reports, say you’re planning to work out four times a week until the end of the year. If you know the cold morning weather is going to persuade you to stay under the covers and sleep in, be proactive: Book workout classes online every week so you know they’re in your calendar, and you’re more likely to show up. Also, write down your challenges—like the dropping temps preventing you from leaving your house—to keep yourself accountable, Carmichael adds.

Picture yourself on January 1 having been successful with your Winter Arc Challenge, then move backward and think about everything that led up to it. If your significant goal was to do a yoga class every week, visualize yourself walking through the snow to get to your Monday night class, or doing a virtual class at home when there was a bad blizzard. Also think about when you almost skipped classes and fell off the wagon, but you used thought replacements to continue reinforcing your goals. Using imagery will help you mentally prepare for the journey ahead, Carmichael notes.

Ask around to see if any of your friends are also doing the Winter Arc Challenge—or if they’re willing to hold you accountable. Then, proposal regular meetups or calls to check in. “Talk about how things went with a promise to be honest and supportive if one or both of you is falling off,” Carmichael says. “It will help you to stay consistent when you can leverage your social support network.”.

Recent findings suggest that no matter when you started the Winter Arc Challenge, you’ll see and feel the benefits of bettering yourself in no time. Good luck—you got this!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • MEN’S HEALTH EDITORS spend a lot of time outdoors.
  • Recent findings suggest that as someone who tests gear year-round—and as part of a team that’s been reviewing winter coats since 2019—I’ve worn everything from lightweight puffers on frosty commutes to parkas in sub-zero conditions.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve been getting my wear out of Mack Weldon’s WarmKnit Air Hooded Jacket for the past year and it surprised me with its performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MEN’S HEALTH EDITORS spend a lot of time outdoors. We commute to our NYC office, then juggle the gym, errands, and weekend outings. So when cold weather hits, we need winter coats that can get us through nearly every icy scenario imaginable. Gone are the days when staying warm meant looking like a walking snowman. Today’s outerwear pairs advanced insulation with weather-resistant fabrics and thoughtful details to help keep you warm when the temperatures drop. The best designs layer comfortably, move well, and still look sharp.

Recent findings suggest that as someone who tests gear year-round—and as part of a team that’s been reviewing winter coats since 2019—I’ve worn everything from lightweight puffers on frosty commutes to parkas in sub-zero conditions. Along the way, the Men’s Health style team has put more than 40 coats through real-life use: daily city commutes, snowy trail days, and ski trips. We look at how warm they actually feel, how well they move, how tough the materials are, and whether they look good off the rack. And after all that, Mack Weldon, Columbia, and Canada Goose rose to the top as the best winter coats for men.

It has been revealed that I’ve been getting my wear out of Mack Weldon’s WarmKnit Air Hooded Jacket for the past year and it surprised me with its performance. At first glance, you’d think it’s just a lightweight puffer built for those mild 50- to 60-degree temps. But I found it could hang in the 40s, too—and still keep me warm. That’s thanks to its Thinsulate fill, synthetic insulation made of ultra-fine fibers, which does the heavy lifting without making me feel like a bloated marshmallow. It’s water- and wind-resistant, so a little drizzle or gusty wind doesn’t ruin a commute either.

Sources indicate that the snap-button front and the two-way zipper make it easy to get in and out of, and the structured hood actually stays put, protecting your head without flopping around or blowing off. Just like most of Mack Weldon’s winter collection, sporty casual meets performance is the vibe here, so you can wear it with anything from a sweatsuit to a casual crewneck over chinos. With bonded quilting and interior pockets, it's both functional and polished, so it works for weekend hikes or casual dinners.

Industry observers note that that said, there are trade‑offs. The jacket’s waist‑length cut means it won’t cover your core the way a mid‑thigh parka does, so in truly cold winter conditions you’ll feel more exposed around hips and lower back. If you need serious warmth for winter storms, opt for a longer cut; if you want a versatile everyday coat for mild to moderately cold weather, this is a standout value pick.

For days when you want warmth without the bulk, this Columbia down jacket delivers in spades. It uses Omni‑Heat reflective lining—those tiny silver dots that bounce your body heat back at you—which helps keep heat where you want it even as temperatures dip and winds pick up. It’s the kind of jacket you reach for when you want to feel cozy without feeling weighed down.

Industry observers note that the 650‑fill down has enough loft to stay warm without ballooning your silhouette, and the baffle construction keeps insulation evenly distributed while creating a streamlined look that’s more polished than many puffers of similar warmth. Columbia also packs in tech‑forward features like HeatSeal construction to trap warmth while still allowing breathability and Omni‑Shield for moisture resistance and stain repellency—handy when you’re trudging through slush or, as I once did, surviving a spilled coffee on the way to the bus.

What I appreciate most is how easily it layers: It slips over a fleece or hoodie without feeling stiff, and it’s comfortable enough to wear all day whether you’re heading to work or exploring snowy trails. It’s not the warmest jacket around, but for everyday winter conditions where you want mobility and comfort with insulation, it’s a fantastic pick.

It has been revealed that this is, quite simply, one of the best budget winter jackets we’ve tested—and it’s worth your attention even if you usually steer clear of ultra‑affordable picks. Deals and Trends Editor Tim Kohut wore the coat zipped up, and found that the heavyweight insulation did a solid job at keeping the shivers at bay on a brisk walk to the train — all without overheating once he hit the warm subway platform.

According to recent reports, the polyester shell is water-repellent, not waterproof, so he can survive light showers without them soaking through to his clothes. It may not be the best option for heavy rain, so if you’re staring down a prolonged rainstorm, an umbrella or rain layer is still a smart call. Its relaxed fit is roomy enough for you to fit a chunky sweater underneath without bulk. Kohut rocked a T-shirt and chunky cardigan, and did not feel like the Michelin Man after being fully zipped up. The hood doesn’t cinch tight — one of the few real drawbacks — which lets cold air sneak in on windier days, but it is fleece‑lined for extra comfort and warmth.

Sources indicate that pockets are straightforward but functional, and the simple styling means this jacket works for daily commuting as easily as casual weekends. For the price, it’s a total win if you want something warm, reliable, and unfussy without dropping substantial cash.

Our Grooming Editor Sean Zucker wore this parka in every cold-weather situation: long commutes, chilly hikes, snowball fights. It has a slim puffer design but with a longer cut and more down, making it warmer for bone-chilling morning walks to the coffee shop. Zucker recently got caught in a sudden downpour, and the waterproof—not just water-resistant—shell kept him completely dry. On a freezing 30-degree cold and windy day, he stayed warm and comfortable the entire time. Plus, the storm cuffs blocked icy gusts from sneaking in at the sleeves.

Sources indicate that he also appreciated the two-way zipper, which you don’t see on a lot of winter coats. It made hopping on and off the subway or sitting at a café easy without feeling restricted. While the insulated hood isn’t super spacious, it cinches close enough to trap heat. The fit is stylish without feeling bulky, and his hands fit perfectly in the pockets—small detail, but it really makes a difference when it’s freezing out. Yes, it’s an investment piece, but with premium 700-fill down warmth, waterproof and windproof protection, and thoughtful features, this parka is a true workhorse built to handle harsh conditions.

In a recent development, canada Goose’s coat may come with some sticker shock, but our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan has made good use of it for the past three winters. He wears it to walk his two corgis, and between the snow, wind, and icy sidewalks, it keeps him warm without feeling like he’s lugging around a heavy sleeping bag. The Arctic Tech fabric—a polyester-cotton blend—has structure without stiffness, so it handles those brutal days when the wind tries to cut straight through you. Its longer silhouette offers extra coverage in snowy conditions. Not to mention, it’s a stylish coat, so you’re getting warmth and thoughtful design versus a bulky, shapeless puffer.

According to recent reports, like Fjallraven’s parka, this one has more pockets than your average coat—four outside, three inside. Two are great for thawing frozen mitts, and the others have flaps that help secure smaller essentials like a wallet, beanie, or winter gloves. There’s even a down-filled hood that feels toasty without making you feel stuffy, plus backpack-style straps if you want to carry it hands-free while running errands or grabbing coffee.

According to recent reports, sure, it’s very pricey, but we had to bite the bullet and think about the bigger picture. Stepping outside doesn’t feel like wrestling with the elements anymore. Between warmth, thoughtful design, and sleek style, it’s become our go-to armor for extreme weather—and it’s already survived three ruthless winter seasons in a row.

Men’s Health designer Jason Speakman took this burly parka from Fjallraven out on the slopes during a trip to Aspen. At 6 feet tall with a slender build, he found that this jacket wasn’t suffocating or too heavy, letting him flex, bend, and twist easily while carving turns or easing down steep trails. The fleece-lined hood with detachable faux fur edging kept his head and ears warm on icy chairlift rides, and he could easily remove the fur for a sleeker après-ski look. Thanks to the drawcords at the neck, it pulls tight around your face to shut out breezes.

This coat has eight pockets—more than any on the list—including roomy zippered chest pockets that fit slim essentials like a phone or cardholder. Its weight-to-warmth ratio is excellent; after five hours on the snow, Speakman stayed warm without feeling like he was wearing a stiff, overstuffed parka. The fit is generous, allowing space to pile base layers and still keep a clean profile.

Down and synthetic insulation are two of the most common options.

Sources indicate that synthetic insulation is made from polyester fibers, more affordable than down, and handles wet weather better. Popular options include PrimaLoft and Thinsulate, which use a blend of synthetic fibers designed to trap heat while remaining lightweight and breathable.

Down is made from clusters of goose or duck plumage, and is prized for its lightweight warmth. It compresses easily for packing and offers superior heat retention in dry conditions. Some coats even blend down and synthetic fill to combine the benefits of both.

It has been revealed that look for a waterproof shell, sealed seams, and a protective hood to help keep rain and snow from soaking through. Features like adjustable cuffs and storm flaps can also help block out wind and moisture. If you’re dealing with wet, snowy winters, prioritize a fully waterproof design over a water-resistant finish.

Recent findings suggest that A winter coat should leave enough room to layer a sweater or hoodie without feeling bulky or restricting movement. The shoulders should sit comfortably, the sleeves should cover the wrists, and the hem should provide enough coverage for your needs. If you strategy to wear it over heavier layers, consider sizing up, but always check the brand’s fit recommendations.

Look for fleece-lined hand pockets to keep your fingers warm and interior pockets to protect your phone, wallet, or AirPods from the cold. Extra details like zippered or hidden pockets add practicality, especially for commuting, travel, or outdoor adventures.

Our fashion team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, tested more than 40 winter coats in real-world conditions, from freezing city commutes to snowy hikes, ski trips, and travel days spent shuffling between cold-weather airports. If a coat claimed to handle winter, we made sure it proved it. We focused on warmth, durability, fit, mobility, and practicality. We paid attention to how each coat insulated in different temperatures, whether the materials could stand up to wind and wet weather, how well the coat moved with us during long days out, and whether the design felt useful rather than overbuilt.

Details like pocket placement, zippers, adjustability, and overall comfort played a significant role too. After months of wear and side-by-side comparisons, only the top performers made our final list. These are the winter coats that stayed warm, held up, and made our lives easier—not just in theory, but in brutal winter reality.

In a recent development, for most of us, the terms "jacket" and "coat" are probably interchangeable. However, the main difference comes down to length and coverage. A winter coat's main objective is to keep you warm, which is why it's bigger and thicker, extends past the hips or toward the knees, and is filled with some type of insulation. A jacket, on the other hand, is considered a combination of style and warmth. Jackets don't typically go past the waist and they're designed to be worn indoors at times. Winter jackets can be layered more with outfits too—sometimes even under a coat.

Recent findings suggest that winter jackets can work as your main outer layer in cold weather, especially when they’re insulated and long enough to provide adequate coverage. For colder temperatures or extended time outdoors, a longer, more heavily insulated coat or parka can provide additional warmth and protection. The right choice ultimately depends on the weather, your activity level, and how much you plan to layer underneath.

The coolest ride in town is England’s first electric ice cream truck

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it indicates it’s open for orders for more.
  • Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.
  • And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it indicates it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”.

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?).

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A GREAT PAIR of sunglasses is the easiest way to upgrade your look.
  • Recent findings suggest that since 2020, our Men’s Health fashion team has tested over 50 styles—including aviators, wayfarers, and rounded frames—which all have stood the test of time due to their durability, versatility, and style.
  • Recent findings suggest that as a style editor for the past four years, I’ve tested over 25 different pairs of sunnies, but the Ray-Ban Wayfarer is still the best in its class.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GREAT PAIR of sunglasses is the easiest way to upgrade your look. The right style can sharpen angular faces, soften sharper ones, or dress up even the most basic outfit—think square frames adding structure to a round face, or classic aviators elevating a T-shirt and jeans. They also protect your eyes from UV rays and cut down on glare, so you’re covered in both style and function. When picking your next pair, think about face shape and classic silhouettes.

Recent findings suggest that since 2020, our Men’s Health fashion team has tested over 50 styles—including aviators, wayfarers, and rounded frames—which all have stood the test of time due to their durability, versatility, and style. And don’t forget about occasions—what you wear to the beach, on a hike, or just around the city should match both your lifestyle and how you want to show up.

Recent findings suggest that as a style editor for the past four years, I’ve tested over 25 different pairs of sunnies, but the Ray-Ban Wayfarer is still the best in its class. The signature silhouette—a slightly angular trapezoidal shape with thicker acetate frames—adds structure without looking too sharp, so it looks great on just about all round, oval, and even square faces and plays well with just about every fit.

First introduced in the ’50s as a casual alternative to metal frames, it was later worn by Tom Cruise, Michael Jackson, and George Michael, cementing its style icon status by the ’80s. In the past few years, Ray-Ban has updated it with a few stylish design tweaks—including a slightly smaller frame and more rounded lens shapes. We found it’s even easier to wear day-to-day to the office, lunch, or an early happy hour.

A wide range of frame and lens colors are available in the Original Wayfarer, but you can’t ever go wrong with the old-school black. We love this style because it looks great with every kind of vibe: a tailored suit, a tee and jeans, or just swim trunks on vacation. I found the acetate frame to be extra robust and heavy-duty at withstanding impact, courtesy of the seven-barrel hinges on each side. While this design does make the whole thing a bit heavier than most sunnies on this list, I never feel like it’s a burden on my face. I’ve found them comfortable whether I’m wearing them for a couple hours or from sunup to sundown.

Read More: Best Sunglasses Brands for Men.

In a recent development, the Downing from Warby Parker is a safe bet because it will never go out of style. The slightly rounded shape traces back to midcentury optical styles that leaned more circular before chunkier shapes took over the game. That softer, more classic silhouette flatters square to angular face shapes especially well, and gives the Downing its staying power today. While heritage brands like Ray-Ban and Persol offer similar rounded styles, Warby Parker delivers a comparable timeless look and build at a much more accessible price.

According to recent reports, the rounded lenses help soften sharper, more angular faces, but they’re not overly circular, which is why they still work on round and oval faces too. It’s one of those rare shapes that’s versatile across the board. I have a round face, and they look great with whatever vibe I’m going with. The keyhole bridge sits naturally on the nose (no adjustable pads), though it may not be a perfect fit for guys with lower or higher nose bridges. The acetate frame feels smooth yet durable, and the scratch-resistant lenses hold well if you drop them or toss them in your bag.

Recent findings suggest that I also found that the temples are lightweight, so they don’t pinch behind your ears, making them easy to wear from the time I get to the office to the time I leave. The color—called English Oak—is like a toned-down tortoise that looks best with solid, everyday staples.

It has been revealed that if you want a pair of sunglasses that you can throw on with anything, every day, The Napoli is the one. I’ve worn them with everything—think T-shirt and jeans, a polo and chinos, or even a hoodie and shorts. The square shape adds structure to rounder faces without looking too boxy on guys with sharper features. The keyhole bridge sits so comfortably on the nose, I don’t even feel it. I love the lens colors, which veer away from the super dark black lenses.

In a recent development, the gradient brown-to-yellow lenses are easy on the eyes in bright sun, giving a relaxed vibe. This also makes the sunnies more wearable—you can rock them in the bright sun or just walk around the city without feeling like you’re hiding behind your shades. The temples are slim but stay in place no matter how I move my head. While the acetate frame is lightweight and comfortable, it doesn’t offer the same durability as heavier acetate, so handle with care if you’re rough on glasses or tend to toss them in your bag.

Industry observers note that randolph began churning out military-spec aviators for the U.S. Air Force in the late 1970s, and its metal frames are still very stylish today. Unlike mass-produced sunglasses, each pair is handcrafted in the U.S., going through 200 steps over six weeks, which gives them a high-quality feel built to last a lifetime. I’ve had mine for three years now and wore them for the first time during a weekend getaway to Nantucket. I sported them on boat rides, walking along the pier, and during casual dinners. They performed flawlessly, reducing glare on the water and staying comfortable for hours. They’re perfect for everyday casual outfits like shorts, T-shirts, or polo shirts. They also pair nicely with slightly dressier looks, like linen button-downs or lightweight jackets.

It has been revealed that the Skytech glass lenses are made from durable optical glass and deliver exceptional clarity, contrast, and anti-reflective performance, with both polarized and nonpolarized options available. The durable matte chrome frames with snug screws hold up well, while the clear bayonet-style temple tips slide gently along the side of your head instead of curving around your ears. They make the sunglasses easy to slip on and off and help them stay in place. This aviator shape works for most face types but is especially flattering on oval, square, and heart-shaped faces, balancing wider foreheads and softening softer jawlines. It’s not the best option for wider faces as it can make them appear even bigger.

According to recent reports, oakley’s Radar EV Path has those taller lenses perfect for athletes and anyone who spends a lot of time running, golfing, or cycling. This extended range of view really reveals off the legendary Prizm lens, which makes colors pop and boosts contrast so you can see everything clearly. This wraparound design gives you extra coverage at the top, protecting your eyes from sunlight, wind, and debris. The no-slip nosepad and extended arms keep the glasses locked in place, even when you're sweating.

The lightweight, flexible frame plus adjustable nosepiece makes them comfortable for long sessions. Best for oval and medium-to-long faces, the wraparound style hugs the sides for a snug, secure fit. Small or very round faces can still wear them, but wider faces might find them a little tight. Heads-up: These are just made for performance and not style, so don’t try to sport them with a casual T-shirt or button-up at a dressy brunch.

Industry observers note that uniqlo delivers an affordable rectangular pair of sunglasses that don’t feel cheap. They look as sharp and polished as pairs that cost way more. The frames are made from flexible plastic that feel lightweight in hand but aren’t flimsy. Case in point: I dropped them more than once and even accidentally sat on them—fully expecting a snap. Somehow, the temples held strong and didn’t split in half. The thicker temples help here, too. The bridge and nose pads are molded into the frame, providing comfortable support. This pair of sunglasses lacks adjustable nose pads, so the fit may not work for those who have a low or high nose bridge.

The rectangular shape is especially great for rounder or softer face shapes, adding structure and making your features look sharper. If you’ve got a fuller face, this is one of the easiest ways to balance things out. Yes, these shades block sunlight effectively with enough coverage to keep glare out of your eyes without feeling oversized. I wore them on bright midday walks and didn’t find myself having to squint. If you’re looking for multiple color frames, Uniqlo doesn’t offer that with these shades. You can only get them in black, but that doesn’t limit your styling options.

Industry observers note that ray-Ban’s round sunglasses are a step up from your everyday pair, thanks to the gold metal rims and classic green lenses, which give off a more luxe, retro aesthetic. The thin metal build looks great and keeps the pair lightweight and sleek, but it’s more delicate than thicker frames.

Recent findings suggest that the metal bridge with adjustable nose pads lets you fine-tune the fit, while the slim temples keep them comfortable. It’s perfect for vacation fits—easily pairing with swim trunks or an open camp shirt and linen shorts for a resort lunch. I’ve worn mine poolside in Costa Rica while lying in the sun, but they’ll also dress something like a tee and jeans if you don’t want to look too basic. It sits a bit closer to the face (petite fit), which makes it feel more styled than oversized. The round shape softens sharper features, but still works across the board for most guys. Bonus: These Ray-Ban’s come in a bunch of lens options—blue, brown, and gradients—so you can switch up the vibe.

Tortoise sunglasses are timeless, versatile, and universally flattering. This classy pair from Moscot looks good with lots of neutral items—think white tees, navy shirts, or olive chinos. You can also mix it with small or muted patterns like thin stripes, tiny checks, or small prints. These shades are made from real Italian acetate and come in a square-ish round silhouette that’ll always be in style. It’s offered in four sizes for a tailored fit. The keyhole nose bridge keeps them comfortable for more than six hours, and the rims feel robust without feeling overly heavy.

The rounded lenses work best on round and oval faces, thanks to its slight square edge that balances softer features. Caveat: Guys with very square or angular faces may find that the softer edges of this frame don’t add much definition, so the effect is more relaxed than structured. Also, I found these sunnies to be heavier than other picks that I’ve tested, which may feel bulky on smaller faces. They come in over 20 color options, but for an everyday classic look, the chestnut fade is a safe bet.

In a recent development, persol's aviator shades offer a wider field of view and a serious level of coverage. These bold, square sunglasses are a great option for guys with round faces, but anyone can sport them.

In a recent development, in our testing, we found that the polarized, light blue lenses not only looked dope, but also offered scratch and shatter resistance to make sure these sunnies last a while. They look great worn for a lunch date with friends, but give real main character energy when you're tanning on the beach or poolside.

It has been revealed that another stylish but also functional standout is the 100 percent acetate frame, which we've found to be lightweight and sturdy. After using it for a full day at the beach, we hardly noticed that we were actually wearing it.

It has been revealed that rectangular sunglasses tend to look best on guys with rounded, oval, or heart-shaped faces. If that’s you, say hello to Oliver Peoples' version, which is a collaboration with tennis champ Roger Federer. Their sharper edges complement guys with softer facial features.

We found that these sunnies offer high-optical quality as well as style for days spent on and off the tennis court. Thanks to the adjustable rubber nose pads and temple tips, they rested gently on our face (even when we were playing) and felt more comfortable to wear all day long than any other rectangular frames we tested.

Look for frames that add structure—think square, rectangular, or angular aviators and wayfarers. These shapes balance softer features and make your face appear more defined.

Most frame shapes work, from round to square. Experiment with classic aviators, bold wayfarers, or even a round lens for a vintage vibe.

Opt for rounded or oval frames that soften a strong jawline. Circle lenses or softer rectangle shapes can help create balance.

Frames that are wider at the bottom or slightly curved help balance a broader forehead. Aviators, teardrop lenses, or rounded frames are good options.

High cheekbones and a narrow forehead and chin look great with rimless or oval frames of sunglasses because they emphasize your eyes and soften your facial angles.

Industry observers note that when choosing a new pair of sunglasses, you should make sure that they provide 100 percent UV protection against both UVA and UVB rays. Otherwise, you can find yourself in a world of problems. "Excessive sun exposure could lead to cataracts and eye or eyelid cancer," Jeff Pettey, MD, clinical spokesperson for the American Academy of Ophthalmology, previously told MH. You don't have to spend a fortune on sunglasses, but it's a must that you find a pair that fits well. As for what type to consider, go with wraparound models as they block UV rays that come in from the side and shield against winds that can cause dry eyes.

Polarized lenses are designed to cut down harsh glare, which helps reduce eye strain and makes it easier to see clearly in bright conditions. That glare usually comes from light bouncing off flat surfaces like water, snow, or pavement, not just direct sunlight. Polarized technology works by filtering out light, so you’re not squinting or dealing with that blinding shine. Because of that, polarized sunglasses are especially useful for water sports and outdoor activities, while photochromic lenses (which adjust to changing light) are recommended for everyday use.

Finding the right pair of sunglasses has everything to do with a frame that works for your face, style, and how you live in them. Certain shapes can sharpen your features or balance them out, while the right style can pull together everything from a laid-back weekend fit to a more polished look. That’s why we focused on aviators, wayfarers, round, square, and sport frames—the same ones our team has tested across everyday wear, travel, and outdoor activities—so you’re getting options that look good and hold up in real situations.

Recent findings suggest that to find the best sunglasses for men, our Men’s Health fashion team—led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan—has tested over 50 pairs since 2021. That means everything from daily commutes and office fits to tropical getaways, beach days, and long weekends on the water, along with more active use like running, hiking, and biking. We put each pair through the same hands-on process, evaluating style, comfort, fit, durability, and overall value.

We paid close attention to how they held up over time—whether the frames could handle sweat and movement, if the lenses reduced glare and eye strain, and whether they delivered reliable 100 percent UV protection. Just as important, we looked at versatility: Could one pair work across multiple settings, from casual everyday wear to more dressed-up occasions? We also compared them against top competitors in the category to make sure each pick truly stands out in its class. Read on for the best sunglasses for men from classic brands like Ray-Ban and Randolph to newcomers like Jimmy Fairly Paris to sporty ones like Oakley.

Acetate is a popular material for crafting frames since it combines both durability and style, allowing for a wide range of color and pattern options, and is thus frequently used in premium sunglasses. TR-90, a thermoplastic material, is known for its durability, flexibility, and resistance to impact, and thus can often be found in outdoorsy sunglasses. Nylon is lightweight and flexible while offering excellent durability, even being able to resist extreme temperatures. Other materials like stainless steel and titanium are simply no-brainers due to their outstanding durability and ability to withstand wear and tear over time.

The 10 Best Cross-Training Shoes for Women, Tested by Editors

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that OUR FITNESS EDITORS love to slip on cushy sneakers like the Hoka Clifton 11 for our 5Ks and hot girl walks. But on days when we're lifting heavy, doing a functional strength training workout, or have a gym sesh that switches between lifts and sprints, we turn to our favorite cross-training shoes. If you’re unfamiliar with the term, cross-training is combining different exercise modalities—like cardio, resistance training, and plyometric (rapid movements)—during a gym session. Think of these sneakers as multipurpose powerhouses. They keep your feet locked in, whether you’re deadlifting or speed walking on an under-desk treadmill.

Industry observers note that “They’re designed to handle side-to-side movement, quick pivots, and changes in direction—not just forward motion,” claims Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois. “This makes them more supportive for gym workouts, classes, or sports where your foot needs stability in multiple planes, like pickleball or tennis.” On the flip side, a walking or running shoe usually only supports you in straight-line motion, Lockwood says.

Sources indicate that wearing running sneakers for strength training workouts is generally a no-no (except for the caveat about the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 below). All the podiatrists I spoke with say it’s safer and beneficial to invest in cross-training shoes. That’s because they usually have flatter outsoles and thinner midsoles than running shoes to keep your feet locked in, claims Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California. That way, you won’t wobble during your deadlifts and box jumps. The material of cross-training shoes is also more durable than running shoes to resist wear and tear, and has thick heel counters to help prevent ankle injuries.

Whether you're a seasoned weightlifting junkie or a runner on a mission to integrate more training modalities into your routine, read on for the best cross-training shoes you can find.

Industry observers note that after testing dozens of cross-training shoes this past year, the latest lululemon Chargefeel 3 stands out for its impeccable support and stability during speedy, lateral movements like ice skaters, kettlebell squats, and Zumba workouts. We’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Despite the fact that sneaker fit and feel is extremely subjective, everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” says WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

It’s now 8 ounces instead of 9.1 ounces, and has a lower heel-to-toe drop—6 mm compared to 9.5 mm—to help alleviate stress on the ankles and feet. WH associate style and commerce editor Shannen Zitz loves the wider build for lifting and squatting. She states her feet feel locked in and extra secure. “My feet stay securely in place thanks to a forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter,” says Zitz. She also notes that the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

And post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. “I recently wore these while traveling, and they kept my feet super happy power walking through the airport and standing on long security and customs lines,” Zitz adds. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

The fit is true to size, and the breathable knit upper doesn’t feel constricting when wearing thick socks (perfect for combating blisters!). Although wide size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, Zitz notes the wide outsole may feel too bulky during quick and dynamic HIIT workouts.

Read More: Every Lululemon Shoe, Ranked.

We wouldn’t recommend most running shoes for cross-training, but the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is an exception. You can effortlessly transition from long runs to deadlifts, thanks to its balanced cushioning and moderate heel-to-toe drop.

Sources indicate that compared to the GTS 24, the latest version has slightly softer cushioning, with about 3 mm more foam in the forefoot and 1 mm in the heel, giving it a smoother, more comfortable feel underfoot. It also drops from 12 mm to 10 mm, creating a slightly more level feel. That can make it feel more stable during strength work than higher-drop running shoes.

At 9 ounces, it’s a lightweight gem, especially for those with overpronation or flat feet during agility drills. Its GuideRails technology—firm foam on both sides of the foot—keeps feet aligned during everything from Bulgarian split squats to lunges to speed walking. Plus, stiff heel padding keeps feet from sliding."These feel super comfortable and supportive for everyday life, traditional workouts, walks, easy runs—you name it," states Melissa Kendter, CPT, a functional strength coach. "I love that this shoe feels well cushioned but doesn't have a huge chunky sole, making it more appropriate for strength workouts than most running shoes.".

Because the outsole is relatively smooth (it’s built for road miles, not side-to-side gym moves), we’d stick to non-slip floors for quick lateral work. If your workouts are heavy on lifting or plyometrics, a flatter cross-trainer like the Nike Metcon 10 may feel steadier and more secure underfoot.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

We’ve been fans of the Nano series since 2018, and every year we notice Reebok levels up its cushioning and heel stability to keep our feet locked in and comfortable during even the most intense workouts. The midsole padding is firm for balancing during heavy lifts and lateral movements, yet is still bouncy for excellent rebound during HIIT workouts and explosive jumps. The mesh material upper is also firm, keeping you steady when lifting heavy.

MH digital designer Taryn Colbert used to prefer flat lifestyle shoes like Converse or Vans, but has since switched over to the Nano X5 for her cross-training sessions. The stiffer soles offer her better balance, while she notes that the heel counter is dense, meaning it doesn’t flex easily. However, the 7 mm heel-to-toe drop may be too steep for some weightlifters who prefer a ground-feel shoe. But it’s a pro if you like extra heel support.

The grippy outsole delivers superior traction when executing deadlifts or weighted squats, while the snug laces never budge. Colbert also notes that the breathable material helps combat sweaty feet. Just note that the fit runs tight (consider ordering at least a half-size up), and it weighs 12.1 ounces, making it one of the heaviest shoes in this guide.

If your workouts focus on dynamic moves like kettlebell swings or heavy lifting, the Nobull Drive is a gem. It’s crafted with a breathable mesh knit upper that feels sock-like and keeps feet cool during grueling reps.

Sources indicate that the balance of flexibility and firmness makes it simple to transition from the squat rack to the HIIT studio. WH associate editor Olivia Luppino wears them during physical therapy to help maintain balance when doing Bosu ball squats, and then hits the gym to do deadlifts. She also notes the mesh isn’t scratchy—an issue she has had when wearing this material.

In a recent development, the subtle foam feels similar to a minimally-cushioned running shoe, while the low 4 mm drop keeps Luppino grounded when deadlifting. She also notes that a firm heel counter makes her feet feel secure without too much stiffness. And at 8.3 ounces, it’s the lightest shoe in this guide, which makes it an optimal choice for sprints and mixed-modality workouts.

Nike’s latest Metcon 10 is a top pick among our editors when it comes to pumping iron. Its main upgrade compared to the last iteration is a smaller, stiffer plate strategically placed under the heel to help stabilize the feet when squatting heavy reps or doing deadlifts. It’s also lighter at 11.8 ounces (it was previously 13.3 ounces) and feels more responsive during jumps and HIIT when it’s not leg day.

Zitz was completely sold after her first wear. “I feel totally grounded with the 4 mm drop while squatting and lunging, and they never weigh me down while running,” says Zitz. “I also love how sleek and stylish they look (especially in the pink color!), and I've been wearing them with nearly every athleisure fit since I got them.”.

The tough rubber traction is another highlight. It feels almost sticky, helping you stay put. Zitz adds that the grooves on the outsole are great for slick sidewalks or dynamic movements, like box jumps. The mesh upper also offers some breathability, but it’s not the most airy shoe in this guide.

Read More: Best Weightlifting Shoes.

The RAD One V2 is so flexible that it feels like an extension of your feet during lifts, drills, and cardio. The forefoot bends easily and delivers bounce that feels natural. Accardi says her movement feels “controlled, yet free” when these are on her feet. “While firmness is notable in a cross-training shoe, many are too stiff, which limits power in workouts unrelated to lifting,” she says. “These feel nimble yet stable for agility drills and plyometric moves like box jumps.”.

The moderate 6 mm drop and heel counter provide balance and sturdiness. The springy EVA midsole also alleviates joint impact during high-impact moves. And bonus: the cushioning is wrapped with rubber to help combat wear and tear, while the textured outsole provides perfect traction during lateral bounds and tuck jumps. “My footing feels nice and steady during transitions, whether I’m going fast or slow.”.

Note that this kick is the heaviest option in this guide, weighing 12.8 ounces. It’s not the best option for long-distance runs, but it’s a top pick if you’re all about explosive movements.

According to recent reports, on is a cult-fave among runners for its cloud-like outsole that’s become a style statement, but the Cloudpulse Pro proves the brand is also a game changer in cross-training shoes. Besides short sprints, it’s designed for workouts that blend cardio and strength—box jumps, sprints, step-ups, and ice skaters. Its signature CloudTec cushioning—compressive foam that absorbs impact—is ultra-bouncy and makes you feel like you’re flying during jumps and agility drills. It propels you forward whether you’re walking, running, or doing dynamic movements. One word that describes it perfectly is energetic. The foam also isn’t overly soft, which is great for support during fast transitions.

It has been revealed that the 6 mm heel-to-toe drop keeps Accardi grounded and balanced during lateral and dynamic movements. A firm heel counter keeps her feet secure, which gives her the confidence to grind hard. Weighing 10.6 ounces, it feels resilient yet solid. The thick, grippy outsole also helps her maintain control on smooth, slick floors. Plus, the polyester material evaporates sweat to keep feet dry.

It has been revealed that the fit is roomy, especially in the toe box, making it an excellent option for those with wide feet or bunions. “The fit is perfection,” claims WH food producer Tina Martinez. “It’s streamlined through the narrowest part of my foot and hugs my arches in the most secure way.”.

Read More: Best On Shoes for Walking.

If you want a marshmallow-like feel in your cross-training kicks, the While On Earth Move Trainer is a star pick that’s plush minus the bulk. The spongy EVA foam is ideal for short or long runs, while a heel counter (hard plastic that wraps around the heel) prevents any budging during weight training. It’s also light and nimble at 10.6 ounces, making it a workhorse for cardio and strength work.

WH deputy visual editor Dangi McCoy indicates it’s super supportive during at-home workouts and lateral movements like lunges and shuffling. Plus, it requires no break-in period before hitting the gym. “The width of the shoe itself is great for stability—my feet and toes are secure with any movement,” says McCoy. The wide base and toe box offer ample space for natural foot movement, especially during fast circuit training and intervals, while the neutral 6 mm drop promotes even landings.

It has been revealed that another nice feature: It’s stain and water-resistant. While this shoe is comfortable enough for running, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 24 is better for long runs. But sprints and short-distance running workouts? For sure.

Industry observers note that weekly cross-training puts wear and tear on your shoes, so picking a durable pair is a priority. The GORUCK Ballistic Trainer is strong and resilient enough to handle demanding training from plyometrics to climbing. The Cordura nylon upper is abrasion-resistant and strong, while the rubber outsole is thick and sturdy to sustain repetitive force. Accardi has even worn it to rock climb. “The fabric still looks like it did straight out of the box after scraping against a climbing wall,” notes Accardi. “The sole also kept me from slipping on challenging areas.”.

Sources indicate that the 8 mm drop feels level, making it practical for barbell squats or deadlifts, while the EVA foam midsole is plush enough to absorb impact during sprints and jumps. And don’t worry—it doesn’t skimp on stability. A heel counter secures the feet to the insole during weight-bearing exercises. As for fit, a wide toe box allows for comfy movement.

Nike took the best traits of its iconic Free running shoe to create the Metcon 6—a trusty hybrid running and cross trainer. Whether you’re executing agility drills, speed work, or lunges, it delivers the perfect combination of comfort and stability, no matter what workout you have on deck. "This is perfect for my training workouts that consist of part speed run intervals and part strength training because of its combination of cushioning and stability," claims Ashley Barnett, NASM-CPT. She adds that it’s great for jumping, strength routines, and mixed workouts. Accardi also loves wearing it during HIIT classes, highlighting its flexibility and responsiveness when transitioning from burpees to high knees.

Sources indicate that compared to the Metcon 10, it has a higher drop at 7.2 mm. While this is a pro in a running shoe, it may mean having less stability during heavy lifts. It’s also worth noting that it fits snug and narrow, so you may have to go up a half size. Accardi has bunions and had to size up to prevent the fabric from rubbing against the sides of her feet during runs and agility drills.

According to recent reports, everyone has a unique foot shape, and each brand can fit differently. So, finding the right fit can be complex. But as a general rule of thumb, your feet should feel supported, not suffocated, and you shouldn't be counting down the minutes until you can kick them off, notes Mali Pelham, CPT, C.F.S.C., a personal trainer at Wattage in Chicago.

An easy way to measure if you have enough space is by being able to slide your finger back and forth at the back of the heel. Also, your shoes shouldn’t feel like they’re pinching the middle of your foot—this can lead to tingling and numbness if they’re too tight. If you’re completely unsure, it doesn’t hurt to get fitted at a shoe store. Referencing brands’ sizing charts can also be helpful. Also, pay attention to width, as different brands offer narrow and wide options.

Heel-to-toe drop refers to the height difference between the heel and the forefoot of the shoe.

Consider the type of workouts you'll be tackling in your new kicks. Each demands specific qualities in a shoe, though the best cross-training shoes for women are versatile enough to let you do all these workouts in them.

It has been revealed that the Women’s Health team has spent almost seven years (since 2018!) testing and curating the ultimate guide to the best cross-training shoes for women by putting more than 50 cross-training shoes through their paces. Our rigorous testing process involved multiple phases, including scouring reviews, consulting industry experts, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We laced up cross-trainers for a battery of tests designed to assess performance across various activities, including weightlifting, cardio, agility drills, and CrossFit workouts. Then, we evaluated whether or not a shoe is functional for different kinds of workouts, has enough stability to prevent ankle rolling, is durable enough to withstand wear and tear, and is comfortable for long hours at the gym.   • Juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a latest, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core.

  • Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a latest, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The upcoming Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

According to recent reports, teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

The launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The manufacturer was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a latest generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

Sources indicate that the standard Scrambler Hardtail debuted earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

In a recent development, the Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

According to recent reports, battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

Sources indicate that juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Recent findings suggest that even so, notable features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

While the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

Sources indicate that and with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

According to recent reports, the Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced states preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

According to recent reports, at $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • Sources indicate that the largest base IPO deal ever priced at $83 a share Wednesday night, opened Thursday morning at $111.50, and briefly pushed Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.
  • A 17% first-day gain on an $81.34 billion raise is a successful listing by any normal standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Sources indicate that the largest base IPO deal ever priced at $83 a share Wednesday night, opened Thursday morning at $111.50, and briefly pushed Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion. The stock finished at $97.17, up 17% from the offer and down 13% from where it opened (it has since fallen about 15% to $88).

A 17% first-day gain on an $81.34 billion raise is a successful listing by any normal standard.

The rest of the market did not fare as well.

The Nasdaq fell 2.06%. The S&P 500 dropped 1.9%. The Dow lost 2.17% and closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. Tech had rallied before the bell on the listing and reversed by the afternoon.

Sources indicate that MD fell 7.73%. Nebius dropped 7.8%. CoreWeave lost 5%. Nvidia slid 3.4% despite beating earnings last week. Oracle, Micron, Broadcom and Microsoft all finished lower. The biggest AI listing in history happened, and AI infrastructure was the worst place to be holding.

Joe Maher at Capital Economics put it plainly: “Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks.”.

In a recent development, crypto went with it. Bitcoin fell to $61,500, its lowest since early July. That’s a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be the longest run since the nine-week stretch in 2022. Eth hit the $1,750 level, down 28% in thirty days. Gold fell to a fourteen-month low. Silver dropped 3%.

When Bitcoin, equities and gold all sell off on the same session, the common factor is usually the discount rate.

That’s the Fed. Chris Waller spent this week making the case for fifty basis points in December, and the minutes revealed he isn’t alone. FxPro’s Alex Kuptsikevich described the market as spooked by “the spectre of a double rate hike” and pointed out Bitcoin is now more than 7% below its 200-week moving average, the deepest it has traded below that line in three years.

So where does this leave us heading into next week?

Start with what an $81 billion IPO actually does to a market. That money came from somewhere. Add the separate $26 billion private placement from Nvidia, Google, AMD and four other suppliers, and roughly $107 billion of capital got committed to a single name in one day. Kuptsikevich raised the possibility that the listing absorbed the riskiest money in the system, and that if so, some of it rotates back out once the allocation settles.

According to recent reports, that’s the bull case for crypto over the next few weeks. It requires the Fed to cooperate.

For the bear case, one can simply look at SpaceX.

SpaceX priced at $135 in June, opened at $150, and closed its first day up 19%. Then it kept running, hitting $225.64 four days later, up 67% from the offer. The unwind started the following session. By June 22 it had fallen 16% in a single day and sat 31% off the high. By mid-July it traded below its IPO price. By late July it was down roughly 50% from the peak.

That would project out to a market low around Christmas time, which is actually how the 2018 midterm cycle played out. Will history repeat itself? We will find out soon enough. In the interim, expect volatility.
