Experts Warn That a Deadly Disease That Causes ‘Immune Amnesia’ Is Surging in the U.S.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this week, the United States officially lost its measles elimination status, after 26 years.
  • But measles cases have surged in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, doctors fall squarely into the “very concerned” camp for a few reasons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this week, the United States officially lost its measles elimination status, after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which oversees measles elimination status, said in a statement on Tuesday that the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico, “lost their status after the same measles virus lineage circulated uninterrupted for 12 months or more.”.

But measles cases have surged in the U.S. throughout 2026. The most recent CDC surveillance stats on measles report 5,412 confirmed cases in the country, with 47 states affected. Given that measles hasn’t been a large problem in America for decades, it’s fair to be unsure what to think right now.

In a recent development, doctors fall squarely into the “very concerned” camp for a few reasons. “Measles is not a trivial infection,” notes William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine.

Not only can measles be miserable to experience, but it can also cause lingering effects that can lead to everything from deafness to brain infections, Dr. Schaffner points out. Measles can even cause something known as “immune amnesia,” where your body’s immunity to a range of pathogens is basically wiped out. (More on that in a moment.).

Here’s what infectious disease doctors say:.

Meet the experts: Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in Newly introduced York; William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine; and Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

Recent findings suggest that measles, which is also known as rubeola, is a very contagious viral infection, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Measles is so contagious, in fact, that up to 90 percent of people who come into contact with someone with the virus will get it if they’re not protected (like through the vaccine).

Measles usually causes symptoms like a cough, runny nose, tiny spots inside the mouth, a rash, and a high fever. It can also lead to severe complications like pneumonia, immune amnesia, and encephalitis (aka swelling of the brain). “Even with uncomplicated measles, people are usually miserable for a week,” Dr. Schaffner states.

It has been revealed that measles can also cause “immune amnesia,” meaning the virus can wipe out memory B cells and memory T cells that your immune system has built up from previous infections. “There’s a window after having measles where your immune system has taken a hit, and you have increased susceptibility to viruses, pneumonia, and diarrheal illness—it’s a real thing,” says Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in Fresh York. This can last for several months, or possibly even longer, he says.

Industry observers note that again, measles was considered eliminated from the U.S. back in 2000, meaning the virus wasn’t considered to be spreading in the U.S. While the country did see some measles cases, they were usually in people who had visited other countries. However, according to the latest CDC stats, only 18 of the 5,412 confirmed cases were from international travelers this year.

Cases began slowly creeping up last year, with CDC data showing 2,289 cases were reported. This trend continued when, this July, a little over the halfway point of the year, there were already 2,318 cases reported. At the time, Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, noted that this was the highest number of cases seen since the disease was considered eliminated from the country. “Cases were higher only in the early 1990s.”.

Doctors agree that lack of vaccination is the big element behind this increase in cases. “It’s all about vaccination,” Dr. Russo states. “The anti-vaxx movement is more potent now, and they’re winning.”.

With fewer parents giving their children the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, measles cases are creeping back up, Dr. Russo points out.

#29755. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1588 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state.
  • That’s a substantial deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial.
  • Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its fresh Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the organization indicates the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

That’s a substantial deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement shows these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with important conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The new white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”.

The solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

It has been revealed that osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

Sources indicate that the interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The company lists four issues: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

The pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

And 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:.

This is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

QuantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

Industry observers note that but this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

The press release says “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper indicates that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”.

In a recent development, batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

“Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

That’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

Recent findings suggest that the “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS says high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

The business model is the bigger story.

According to recent reports, quantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS says it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

Sources indicate that that fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and announced a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

According to recent reports, there’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper claims the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

In a recent development, everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD looks small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, stated in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

Sources indicate that none of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

Recent findings suggest that this is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

In a recent development, the cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

Industry observers note that key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

Sources indicate that also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

But you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have mentioned so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

So QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

The question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production looks lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Anthropic mathematician states Claude helped him crack the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old puzzle with a $1 million prize attached.

His claim surfaced Friday, one day after the AI company’s stock-market debut, and has not yet been independently verified.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpöge wrote in a four-page note. He says the method also resolves the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which extends the question to other mathematical functions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In a recent development, alpöge says he and Claude encoded their argument in Lean, software used to check mathematical proofs step by step. His note links to 14 downloadable parts of the proof archive, but its availability does not amount to acceptance by the mathematical community.

Alpöge says he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about a possible announcement “late Sunday night,” November 15. He then consulted company leadership and stated there was a constraint to respect, without explaining precisely what it was.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he acknowledged. Alpöge rejected a cynical interpretation of the timing, but did not explicitly say the company’s IPO caused the delay.

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday, November 19, after raising $81.34 billion in its offering.

According to recent reports, alpöge figured in September’s AI math wars. OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem as he and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster pursued related fluid-equation work, sparking a credit dispute over research priority.

In a recent development, openAI followed in October with 722 manuscripts generated by an unreleased model, grouped into 372 families of results. Only 162 included Lean-checked main results, and mathematicians demanded stronger evidence rather than accepting the firm’s flood of claims at face value.

Industry observers note that some mathematicians fear a “mathocalypse,” with AI solving coveted problems before researchers can learn from pursuing them. Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt warned that, without adaptation, “there’s just no more math in 50 years.” At an MIT panel this week, Buckmaster argued mathematics still requires human understanding.

First posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

In a recent development, lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Anthropic previously reported progress on the zeta function without claiming to solve the full hypothesis. Alpöge’s new assertion goes far beyond that earlier work.

In a recent development, the Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Riemann hypothesis among its Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award. Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.

The Healthiest Thing You Can Do for Your Prostate at Age 50

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, so you’d think doctors would be adamant about screening guys for it.
  • According to recent reports, many guys didn’t know whether they should get it or not.
  • In a recent development, the American Cancer Society just came out with fresh guidelines that for the first time, unequivocally say that men should get the screening test.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, so you’d think doctors would be adamant about screening guys for it. Yet for years, prostate cancer screening via the PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test has been plagued by vague recommendations, and some back-and-forth messaging that flipped between “get it” and “the benefits might not be worth it.” Until recently, organizations including the American Cancer Society (ACS) used to give a recommendation that at age 50, guys should talk with their doctors about screening, then engage in a process of “shared decision-making” about whether to get the test.

According to recent reports, many guys didn’t know whether they should get it or not. Without a clear recommendation, it was easy for some to think this PSA blood test wasn’t very vital to do at all. The landscape has changed.

In a recent development, the American Cancer Society just came out with fresh guidelines that for the first time, unequivocally say that men should get the screening test. Guys at average risk should start at age 50. Guys at higher risk (more on that later) should start at 45.

Why that’s a significant deal: “The new guideline not only gets rid of shared decision-making, which is really difficult to execute, is subject to bias, and is really time-intensive,” says Yaw Nyame, MD, of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center at the University of Washington Medical Center. “But it couples that with a better understanding of what present-day prostate cancer screening is.”.

Sources indicate that today, the PSA test is “just the first step, not the final answer,” says William Dahut, MD, chief scientific officer at ACS, and a contributing author to the guidelines. “It is a simple blood test, and an elevated result does not automatically mean cancer of the need for a biopsy.” Many more tools including MRIs and biomarkers help physicians drill down on who needs additional testing. “Our goal is to find prostate cancer earlier, while avoiding unnecessary procedures and treatment,” Dr. Dahut adds.

Recent findings suggest that what changed that prompted the revised recommendations? “It’s vital to understand that guidance evolves as the evidence does,” claims Dr. Dahut. Research has piled up to indicate that PSA screening reduces prostate cancer deaths.

“We do not need to make a disclaimer that maybe you should, maybe you shouldn’t do it. Everyone should do it and you should start early, especially if you have a higher risk of cancer,” states Dr. Nyame, who was on the expert panel that reviewed the upcoming ACS screening guidelines.

In a recent development, while all men should get the test, according to the new guidelines, it’s not a “one size fits all” screening recommendation, Dr. Nyame explains. Recommendations vary according to risk. Find your category and screen according to that.

These are the new ACS guidelines for who and when:.

Other prostate screening guidelines came out earlier in 2026 from the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society for Urologic Oncology (SUO) that had slightly different recommendations for the age at which you should start screening. What gives? The difference in recommended age and frequency of screening “has to do with how the guideline creators are viewing the different studies that they’re using to support their decision making,” Dr. Nyame says.

It doesn’t mean guys should throw up their hands and do nothing in frustration. “The AUA/SUO and ACS guidelines recognize the benefit of knowing a PSA test result earlier in life. A PSA test in the 40- to 50-year age range is a good predictor of the likelihood someone has or will develop a clinically significant prostate cancer,” says James A. Eastham, MD, chief of the urology service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. A higher level early in life is a strong signal that you need to be really diligent about checking your PSA.

According to recent reports, “We’ve watched prostate cancer incidence increase—especially metastatic cancer, for over a decade now,” indicates Dr. Nyame. “And to know that we have a guideline that is so action-oriented toward reversing that course is really exciting.”.

Marty Munson, presently the health director of Men's Health, has been a health editor at properties including Marie Claire, Prevention, Shape and RealAge. She's also certified as a swim and triathlon coach.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis debuted the upcoming “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis debuted the upcoming “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis mentioned the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”.

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a new realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

Industry observers note that the GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

Sources indicate that as a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

Recent findings suggest that to power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a substantial battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis remarked provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

Sources indicate that and.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”.

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

#29750. Tech Report: There’s a Ton of Conspiracies About Lab-Grown Meat Right Now. Here’s What’s Really True.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: There’s a Ton of Conspiracies About Lab-Grown Meat Right Now. Here’s What’s Really True.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lab-grown meat is having an absolute field day on social media, as tons of outlandish claims and conspiracy theories about it are forming: The lab-grown industry is trying to sneak it into our grocery carts by labeling it as natural meat!
  • It has been revealed that formally known as cultivated meat, lab-grown meat has been in development for more than a decade, but it’s only recently begun to capture mainstream attention.
  • Meet the experts: Elliot Swartz, PhD, is a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lab-grown meat is having an absolute field day on social media, as tons of outlandish claims and conspiracy theories about it are forming: The lab-grown industry is trying to sneak it into our grocery carts by labeling it as natural meat! Here’s why you need to avoid it at all costs! In truth, there’s a lot more to the story, and a ton of those claims are false.

It has been revealed that formally known as cultivated meat, lab-grown meat has been in development for more than a decade, but it’s only recently begun to capture mainstream attention. In 2023, it received regulatory clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Now, it’s beginning to make its way into the market (albeit in limited quantities), claims Steven Surico, RD, a registered dietitian with the Food and Nutrition Department at Good Samaritan University Hospital.

Meet the experts: Elliot Swartz, PhD, is a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute. Steven Surico, RD, is a registered dietitian with the Food and Nutrition Department at Good Samaritan University Hospital. Lauri Wright, RDN, is a registered dietitian and associate professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of South Florida College of Public Health.

As such, lab-grown meat is becoming a grossly misunderstood concept. (Cue: The recent influx of misleading social media videos and AI-generated content.) These posts can blur the line between fact and fiction, leaving consumers unsure of what’s real, scaring them when there’s nothing to be afraid of. “The concern is that cultivated meat is something highly artificial, when in reality, it’s not,” says Surico.

Here’s everything you need to know about lab-grown meat, including what it is, whether it’s being sold in stores, and if you should truly worry about it, according to experts.

Cultivated meat is grown directly from animal cells, as opposed to natural meat that’s produced by raising and slaughtering an animal, says Elliot Swartz, PhD, a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute.

“A small sample of cells is fed basic nutrients, like amino acids, fats, vitamins, salts, and sugars, in clean, controlled environments similar to those used to make yogurt, cheese, and beer, where the cells are grown and developed into meat or seafood,” he explains. As the cells multiply and develop, they form the muscle and other tissues that make up meat. Once mature, Swartz claims they’re harvested and prepared as a product that should, at least in theory, offer the same taste, smell, texture, and consistency as ordinary meat.

Lab-grown meat vs. plant-based alternatives: “Beyond Meat products are made primarily from plant ingredients and do not contain animal muscle cells, whereas cultivated meat starts with animal cells and grows those cells into animal tissue,” Surico says.

Recent findings suggest that cultivated meat may address some of the challenges associated with natural meat production, particularly when it comes to food safety, public health, nutrition, and the environmental impact of raising livestock. According to Swartz, one of the biggest advantages is the greater control over the production process, which could offer significant food safety benefits.

Research shows that raising large populations of animals in close quarters can create opportunities for bacteria, other pathogens, and diseases to spread. This can increase the risk of transmission to humans through food (or animal) contact, but cultivated meat could help reduce these risks, Swartz explains.

It has been revealed that cultivated meat is also better for the environment by reducing the land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions needed for meat production. Research from The Good Food Institute even suggests that if cultivated meat can be produced commercially in large quantities using clean energy, it could have a significantly smaller environmental footprint than conventional meat.

Finally, because the cells are grown in a controlled environment, researchers can influence the nutritional composition of the meat, says Lauri Wright, RDN, a registered dietitian and associate professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. For example, they can adjust the amount and types of fat in the meat to reduce saturated fat and cholesterol while increasing desirable nutrients like protein, she explains. Theoretically, this could lead to healthier meat that tastes the same, studies suggest.

While some people are afraid of lab-grown meat because they’re not really sure what’s in it, each product undergoes extensive testing by the FDA and USDA. So, its nutritional content is thoroughly tested to ensure it meets food safety standards, adds Swartz.

Yes, but availability is extremely limited. Cultivated meat has received approval from the FDA and USDA for sale in the U.S., as well as in Singapore and Australia, per The Good Food Institute. However, regulatory approval doesn’t necessarily mean that products are widely available. Plus, eight states in the U.S. have enacted bans or temporary restrictions on cultivated meat, including Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Mississippi, Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, and Texas. These restrictions are largely driven by concerns about protecting traditional agriculture and livestock industries.

Industry observers note that so, contrary to what social media might have you believing, cultivated meat isn’t something you can pick up at your local supermarket just yet. In the U.S., the only product presently being served is Wildtype’s cultivated salmon, which is available at a handful of select restaurants in Washington D.C., Oregon, Arizona, and California.

While it’s difficult to predict exactly when lab-grown meat will be in grocery stores, Swartz expects a gradual rollout, with smaller, more specialized retailers being the first to carry it. “You could start to see cultivated meat products more widely introduced in higher-end retailers in the early 2030s, but I don’t think you’ll see it in substantial box grocery stores until the late 2030s,” he states.

In grocery stores, it’ll be clearly labeled as lab-grown or cultivated meat. “Due to the USDA regulations and labeling, it should be very clear to the consumer if they are buying regular meat or lab-grown meat,” states Surico. In fact, federal law prohibits food from being misbranded or carrying false or misleading labels, and regulators have stated cultivated meat products must be clearly and accurately labeled.

Industry observers note that as for the price, that remains to be seen. Cultivated meat is currently more expensive to produce than most conventional meat and seafood, but Swartz indicates the long-term goal is to bring production costs down to match or fall below those of conventional options.

Not very. “You should not be freaked out,” states Wright. “If anything, you should see it as potential, because the future of lab-grown meat could give consumers more options and alternatives to what they buy and put into their body.”.

Swartz agrees, pointing out that the benefits go beyond offering another way to produce meat. “Whether you care about the environment, animal welfare, food safety, or public health, there’s a lot of potential benefits for cultivated meat that are additive in terms of value for the consumer,” he indicates.

Of course, that doesn’t mean everyone has to embrace cultivated meat—traditional meat isn’t going away or being phased out of grocery stores or restaurants. The goal is simply to give consumers another option, not replace the foods they already know and enjoy. And if cultivated meat isn’t your jam, that’s perfectly fine, too.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1980 w)

Hästens 2000T Mattress, Tested and Reviewed (2026)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, from the moment I touched down in Sweden, the focus was on sleep.
  • According to recent reports, the Swedish manufacturer, which has been making beds since 1852, sits atop the luxury market for mattresses.
  • Sources indicate that but what earns a mattress luxury status?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, from the moment I touched down in Sweden, the focus was on sleep. Coming off a red-eye flight from Upcoming York with only two hours of rest (three if we’re being generous), there was nothing more I wanted to do than lie down. Luckily, a Hästens mattress—the reason for my trip—awaited me at the hotel and soon provided what was perhaps the most luxurious nap I’d ever experienced.

According to recent reports, the Swedish manufacturer, which has been making beds since 1852, sits atop the luxury market for mattresses. The brand—whose name is Swedish for “the horse’s”—has a consuming commitment to craftsmanship, and its horsehair-filled beds are handmade. That level of focus also comes with a hefty price tag, which is why the brand is perhaps best known by the general public for its presence in celebrity homes (or possibly its cameo in an Emily in Paris episode as the subject of the titular character’s latest marketing campaign). But reputation aside, Hästens knows how to make a damn good bed.

Sources indicate that but what earns a mattress luxury status? And what is it actually like to sleep on one from Hästens? After touring the brand’s main factory in Köping, Sweden, I’ve laid my head on one of its most popular mattresses, the 2000T, for the last few months, all in the name of trying to understand how much money a good night’s sleep is worth.

Price listed is for a queen size bed.

In a recent development, to the average person, horsehair is likely not the first mattress fill material that comes to mind—if it comes to mind at all. Gel, innerspring, memory foam, cotton, or some combination of those are way more common. But horsehair has a historic precedent, having been used in beds for many periods of human history, particularly when horses were the primary mode of transportation.

Much of the present-day reason for using the material comes from a scientific point of view: Horsehair strands are naturally hollow, which Hästens claims “transports any excess heat and moisture from your body during deep sleep.” Additionally, when cut and treated, the strands form a helix shape, which works in conjunction with the metal springs in a bed for a strong base of support.

Exterior of the Hastens factory in Köping, Sweden, designed by British architect Ralph Erskine.

An hour and a half train ride northwest from Stockholm, the small town of Köping is so quiet, you might expect to see a horse roaming the streets—maybe having recently received a haircut to donate to the mattress cause. When thinking of the word factory, one may expect a loud, gigantic warehouse filled with whirring machines and assembly lines moving so rapidly you can hardly see the product before it whizzes past. But the Hästens factory possessed a quite different vibe. Sure, there is still machinery and expansive production areas, but it was fairly quiet, and I felt that the energy was more akin to a pottery studio than an industrial plant: craft-forward, methodical, and with a focus on handmade artistry. In fact, my host told me that only around 100 people work in the main factory, most of whom are from the area, highlighting the manufacturer as a point of pride for the local community.

Walking into the processing room of the factory, I was greeted by a small mountain of horsehair on the floor. It looked much more like a soft version of steel wool than the shiny mane and tail I was envisioning. That’s because the hair is cut down to small strands prior to being integrated into the mattresses. The hair also goes through several disinfecting and processing treatments before it even arrives at the factory. Taking a clump between my hands, I was surprised by its springiness. (And horse girls need not fear about animal welfare: My host for the trip confirmed that their suppliers from farms around the world aren’t killing horses for their hair, the mane and tail cuttings they receive are ethically sourced.).

The blue check pattern, developed by fourth-generation company leader Jack Ryde in 1978, is synonymous with the brand. So much so that a check-laden Mercedes was waiting to drive us from the train station to the factory.

Each layer of horsehair in the mattress is fluffed by hand and placed between sheets of cotton and wool.

In a recent development, every aspect of the bed creation process happens by hand: prepping the layers of wool and horsehair for the filling, arranging and securing steel springs, framing the Swedish pine base. I watched workers build each part of the bed with a devoted level of care. The only fully automated aspect of the bed manufacturing that I witnessed on my tour was stitching a pattern onto the top mattress to give it a signature tufted texture. But even that is hand-sewn on certain bed models.

Quality is tested at every step, and if something isn’t up to par, production restarts. For some models, including the Grand Vividus (at the top of Hästens range), there are only a select few craftspeople who are trained in the production process. Much of the brand’s higher price tag comes down to that heightened level of labor and care. If someone on the team is sick or is simply just working slower on a given day, the production timeline increases to accommodate the quality level that Hästens demands: perfection.

My loaned mattress also included a full set of Hästens bedding.

The 2000T is one of the brand’s best sellers, falling around the middle of their price range.

When it comes to my sleep setup, my mattress was the element that I’d been putting off upgrading for years. I only leveled up my years-old box spring with a mattress topper a few years ago. I tend to prioritize bedding when buying new duds for the bedroom, and because I’m consistently testing various sets of sheets for AD, my focus tends to be on how linens can visually transform a space rather than shift my physical experience. All to say, upgrading to a Hästens was like going from a hand-me-down sedan to a Lamborghini.

It has been revealed that before receiving the loaned mattress for testing, I tried out different models in person at the Manhattan flagship store in NoMad, an experience Hästens coins the Sleep Spa. As a staff member talked me through proper spinal alignment and notable pressure points, I lay on various models in a Goldilocks-esque journey to see which mattress was the right fit. True to Hästens’ superlative level of service, even this part of the process felt curated. Ambient music played, lights dimmed, and I was given two pillows and a duvet for snuggling. The meditative process made me focus on how my body responded to each mattress. As a combination stomach-and-side sleeper—and someone who likes to sit on her bed—I selected the 2000T (in firm) after around an hour of sampling.

Recent findings suggest that despite being a firmer model, the 2000T still contours to my body in a way that I can only describe as cushy. The horsehair filling provides a unique springiness that the compression of memory foam or cotton can’t quite replicate. It sinks in just enough to give my shoulders enough space when I sleep on my side, but is supportive enough to keep my hips from dropping out of alignment for the nights I’m on my stomach.

As I mentioned, I often lounge on bed to read, play video games, or what have you. While facilitating sleep is the primary function of a mattress, I was keen to see how its edge control and support would stand up to this alternative usage. I was surprised by how little back pain I sustained after reading sessions that extended beyond two hours. Because of its reinforced springs at the corners and edges, I could also sit right on the edge of the mattress without feeling like I was going to roll off.

The aspect of the horsehair fill I was most intrigued to test was its claim of moisture and heat-wicking properties. I like to be fully swaddled underneath my duvet, top sheet, and sometimes even another blanket when I sleep, which can be a recipe for waking up sweaty. That hasn’t happened once with the 2000T. The foam topper on my prior bed often trapped heat, and I’d wake up in the middle of the night to rip off some of the layers of bedding in order to cool down. With the Hästens, though, I can be as greedy with my bedding as I want to be without overheating.

The ‘massage’ portion lasted about 10 minutes.

As part of their high bar of customer service, the firm offers a free recalibration program from select stores to help maintain the longevity of the mattress and mitigate any compression concerns. The product care program involves Hästens staffers visiting your home (typically once a year) to flip and massage the mattress—the latter consisting of a person marching back and forth across the mattress to redistribute the fill materials. I can safely say having a grown man in booties walk in circles on top of my bed for 10 minutes was one of the oddest moments of my life, but sleeping on the bed that night, I could feel the difference. While there weren’t any severe lumps formed in my two-month testing period, the process smoothed out any compression in the areas I most often lay.

Recent findings suggest that although I’ve only slept on the 2000T for around two months, I can see a noticeable change in how my body feels after a night’s rest. I struggle with hypermobility and have a family history of arthritis, so I’m on high alert about how my joints feel upon waking up in the morning. On my old bed, I typically awoke with some pain in my hips and a stiff lower back. While sleeping on the Hästens hasn’t fully eliminated any achiness, I essentially ceased needing to do the typical stretching routine I used to perform in the morning in order to get my body ready for the day.

Down pillows were provided by the brand for my loaner bed.

The structure of Hästens beds includes a top mattress and middle mattress, the former mimicking a thick topper.

Industry observers note that as someone who has notoriously bad nighttime habits (like plentiful screen time), I had accepted I’d only be able to expect a low level of restfulness from my sleep. I was content with a solid six hours and low-level of back achiness in the morning, thinking I couldn’t consistently adjust my routine to improve my experience. Sleeping on the Hästens 2000T has changed that mindset drastically. It’s without a doubt the best mattress I’ve ever slept on.

According to recent reports, however, it’s easy for me to say this bed is worth it because I didn’t have to pay the steep price tag of $74,780 to try it out in my home. Yes, Hästens exceeded my expectations when it came to sleep, but after the testing period ends, I don’t anticipate a sudden change in my finances that would allow me to invest in my own 2000T. Although the brand’s beds are built to last a lifetime, and we spend a third of our lives asleep, the question of how much a good night’s sleep is really worth is highly individualized.

This experience more broadly made me consider where we are most willing to invest in when it comes to our home spaces. Sure, a covetable mattress like one from Hästens may not be as flashy as other substantial-ticket purchases, like a giant flat screen, but I’d posit a splurge has few better use cases than on something you return to each night.

#29745. Latest Update: Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (894 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • In a recent development, both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • It has been revealed that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters noted Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg.

In a recent development, both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters claims the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

It has been revealed that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

Recent findings suggest that it was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

Recent findings suggest that there are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

According to recent reports, not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

It has been revealed that leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

According to recent reports, I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and remarked that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

According to recent reports, also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

In a recent development, so the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

Sources indicate that that’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

#29743. Latest Update: Michelle Yeoh on Strength, Stunts, and What Makes Us Human

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2211 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Michelle Yeoh on Strength, Stunts, and What Makes Us Human

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an action hero used to have to be significant and brawny and brusque.
  • Starring as Olwen, a bioengineered artificial human (or “replicant,” as they’re called in the Blade Runner universe, which includes the new series Blade Runner 2099, out November 25 on Amazon Prime Video), the 64-year-old global megastar literally wrestles with people and replicants alike on-screen.
  • But in real life, she dances with even larger issues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an action hero used to have to be significant and brawny and brusque. Michelle Yeoh is none of those things—but you feel her presence and power the instant you meet her. She is kind, warm, and lovely, but she’s also intense…in a really good way. This is a person who listens closely yet also seems ready to launch into a wheelhouse kick at any moment.

Starring as Olwen, a bioengineered artificial human (or “replicant,” as they’re called in the Blade Runner universe, which includes the new series Blade Runner 2099, out November 25 on Amazon Prime Video), the 64-year-old global megastar literally wrestles with people and replicants alike on-screen.

But in real life, she dances with even larger issues. Like what separates humans from the bot world, how we define strength beyond the physical, why we all need to stretch every morning, and, finally, how she gets over a very specific fear. (If you’ve ever watched her in movies like Tomorrow Never Dies or even Everything Everywhere All At Once, you’ll understand how shocking this particular fear is for her. The solution is one six-letter word…and you’ll just have to read on to find out what that is.).

I sat down with Michelle—who is classically trained in ballet and does many of her own martial arts stunts—in NYC for a wide-ranging convo that starts with robots and ends with what she calls the “Michelle prayer.”.

Women’s Health: What was it like to play a replicant, and how did you think about preparing and training for that mindset?

It has been revealed that michelle Yeoh: We have a brilliant writer, Silka Luisa, who had thought out the story for Blade Runner 2099 [a continuation of the original series] and where it has gone. All these replicants are now in charge of a Los Angeles that is no longer what we know. But it’s very interesting because [the question that arises is] What is humanity? The replicants do give the humans hope. As long as you’re good, as long as you do things the way we want them to be handled, you could go to a better place, because now Los Angeles is not exactly the most habitable place.

Sources indicate that replicants are made to look human. In fact, they are flesh and blood, except they’re stronger, faster. They are able to withstand the newly introduced worlds. But empathy is what gives you away as a human. Replicants are born without that emotion. They’re born with memories. They’re given memories to keep them sort of happy and at peace with what they are. Are you born with humanity or does it come with experience and as you live your life with compassion and kindness?

WH: You stated that you’re excited for people to see the series and to share ideas and to talk about it. Is that why? The humanity complexity?

Michelle: The worst is they say, “Oh, yeah, it was interesting.…” What is “just” interesting? Hopefully you go home, you think about it, and then you come back and the next day at work or in school, you’re chatting with your friends— “Well, what are you? A replicant or a human? What would you rather be?”.

WH: How did you prepare, physically, for this role?

Michelle: I think the older you get, the more you have to do to keep up your muscle strength, to keep your muscles there. Without that, you start walking differently. I have the advantage of understanding my body a lot more because I’ve been doing this for the last, well, ever since I was born. I was dancing, doing sports, everything. I do core-strengthening exercises and tai chi every day.

The core was the most important part of the training because we wanted to nail the way Olwen moved. It was with precision. Because if you want to move with motivation, it has to have that strength, that inner strength, rather than just speed. So when you move, it’s almost like you glide. As a replicant, all the moves are sharp, precise, because they’re so strong and powerful. Actually, when you take a human down, it’s too easy. I think all exercises are core-focused. You can’t lift weights or do pilates without working on the core first. Everything has to start from there.

WH: Has your own relationship to risk changed over the years? Are there stunts that you used to do in your 30s that now you’re like “nah,” or do you actually feel more powerful and in control?

Industry observers note that michelle: I think that’s really interesting and a good way of putting it. Feeling powerful doesn’t mean being reckless and silly. I feel more powerful in the sense that I have a better assessment of the risk factors. But naturally, because when I was in my 20s, when I first started out, you’re brave and foolish and you’re also so fit. And I was really, really, really fit at that time because I didn’t have any crazy injuries. And, so, fearless is a good word, but fearless and stupid is not good. That’s a bad combination.

Sometimes the smallest stunts are the worst because you think they’re easy, and then you don’t pay full attention. You’re not focused enough. You’re focused, but you’re like, “Yeah, yeah, yeah. I’ll get it done.” And that’s when something bad will happen.

In a recent development, in the past, when you are beginning, you listen and you do what they tell you to do, and then you have a lot to prove because you don’t want them to think that you’re unable or you’re not capable, so you do it. But now you go, “How about we…” And then you can speak with power because you know your character. And then I’ll go, “But Olwen won’t do it like that.” And who is going to challenge me?

WH: I understand that you became a bit of a mentor to Hunter Schafer. So talk to us a little about the stunt piece.… Did you help her figure out how to have that voice for herself?

Michelle: To be honest, when I look at her, I go, “Oh my god, I see my young self.” When they show her something, she’ll just throw herself into it because she wants to do it. She’s eager to do it. But then I have to keep reminding her, “You don’t have the same kind of training the stunt people have. So when you can’t do it, it doesn’t mean that you’re not good.”.

In a recent development, what I do is try to remind her, like, “Hunter, knee pads, Hunter, elbow pads. What is the stunt that you’re doing? Get them on.” Because sometimes you go, like, No, no, no, it’s okay. It’s not okay. Get it on.

It’s a joy to work with her. It’s just a joy to be with her, which sometimes can be difficult because we’re supposed to be against each other in Blade Runner 2099. I mean, she’s a human pretending to be a replicant, pretending to be a blade runner. But somehow their missions intertwine, so they have no choice but to learn to work together. So we have a lot of fun.

WH: What are your nonnegotiables? What are the things you, Michelle, must do every single day for your health that you are consistent with?

Michelle: Water, sunblock, and a lot of stretching. That is a must.

I do tai chi, I do my ballet and tai chi. I’ve been doing that for a long time now. I try to do that every day because I’ve unfortunately had injuries in the past—my back, my knees, my shoulder. I don’t know where I don’t have an injury. As I’m in bed, I do a lot of stretching. When I wake up, the first thing I do in my bed is to go through the motions so that the body wakes up with the mind and everything comes into place.

I think that’s what you have to find: your own moves [or routine] so that you don’t give yourself an excuse when you go, “Oh, it’s raining. No time to go to the gym.” So you just do it even in the bed, you’re stretching, you’re doing all those core exercises to wake up the mind, to wake up the abs, the back, and the legs, everything. And that helps when we’re actually on-set because then I can step into it and know I am strong and ready to go.

I love being outside, going on hikes. Then if I can’t do that, I’m on the elliptical, because I think cardio is still very important. But now, with time, I do a lot more weights. I’m picking up dumbbells or water bottles, whatever works. You have to combine the strengthening of muscles with cardio exercise.

WH: I’m curious if there’s something that is better now in your 60s than it was in your 20s—anything?

Michelle: I think the only thing that’s a little bit better might be this up here [motions to head].

I do a fairly decent job at keeping up the energy, keeping up the spirits, because I also think it’s the inner strength that is very vital. Your mind is very important. If you don’t have the inner peace, it’s very hard to keep control of your body because negative vibes are the worst thing for any human being. When you have negative vibes around you, in you, then you’re down. I honestly believe that because you’ve gone through so many experiences, you’re better for it. I wouldn’t give that up.

In a recent development, michelle: I have a fear of heights. I know. See, I’m claustrophobic and have a fear of heights.

Michelle: But the magic word is action. Camera rolling…action. And I am focused. Fearless. It’s really, really bizarre. If I don’t hear the word action, then it’s a no go. If I’m in the mall, you know, sometimes you have those walkways that look over the first floor. I walk right in the middle of those. I’m taking no risk. But once action is mentioned on set, I’m good.

According to recent reports, WH: You mentioned a mantra. What, exactly, is it?

Industry observers note that michelle: When I wake up, even before opening my eyes and stretching, I sort of have my own little mantra to wake myself up. I try to talk to my body, thank my body, apologize for anything I’ve done bad, and then welcome everything that’s good because I’m deserving of it.

I don’t sit there and meditate. I don’t understand that at all. Just as long as you feel it yourself that I have what I need for me…because everybody is different.

And that’s why I start my day with a prayer, a mantra. I guess you could call it my own Michelle prayer. Be thankful and be willing to accept anything good that comes your way. I think we have to look at ourselves and have self-worth because I think the inner strength, the inner peace, that sense of compassion and kindness and contentment, is very important. Because if you’re always wanting, needing, and thinking about something else, someone else, then you’re always in conflict, first of all, with yourself.

WH: What does the word strength mean to you? When you hear that word, what’s the definition that comes to mind?

Industry observers note that michelle: I think when you hear that word, first of all, it’s always very top layer. You walk into the gym, I have strength, I have power. I put on a power suit. That’s powerful. But for me, true strength is right in there [points to heart]. Showing weakness is strength. Doing a lot of things that people don’t understand, but for you, when you make a choice, it’s strength. There are so many ways of looking at it, and I don’t think there’s one definition unless you check the encyclopedia and they tell you what it is.

WH: And then we’ll just ignore that and go with the Michelle Yeoh definition anyway.

Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota and Subaru’s fresh electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
  • The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
  • Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s fresh electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

In a recent development, toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

It has been revealed that starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

The Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a latest vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

Sources indicate that you can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

It has been revealed that subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante mentioned the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Thinking about making the switch to an EV? With the 2027 models at dealerships, now could be a good time to find a deal on current 2026 models. You can use the links below to see what’s available at Toyota and Subaru dealerships near you.

#29741. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1353 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that breast cancer awareness has never been higher.
  • Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.
  • But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Sources indicate that dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

It has been revealed that I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

In a recent development, “It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she noted. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

In a recent development, “Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

It has been revealed that for most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss stated. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”.

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she mentioned patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss states that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s crucial to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”.

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”.

It has been revealed that understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she mentioned. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”.

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from latest ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”.

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”.

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”.

According to recent reports, some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

In a recent development, “They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she remarked, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”.

Dr. Weiss claims the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and key, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”.

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and remarked that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:.

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”.

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

It has been revealed that breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”.

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she indicates she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking swiftly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”.

In a recent development, “Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”.

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.
